This paper examines why company law, securities regulation and governance codes do not always prevent board capture, minority shareholder abuse, related-party transaction misuse and disclosure failure in African emerging markets. It adopts a structured doctrinal and comparative corporate governance review, supported by selected case analysis from Nigeria, Kenya, South Africa and Ghana. The paper develops a Legal Accountability Gap framework to show how governance failure occurs when formal duties are weakened by concentrated ownership, weak regulatory capacity, costly litigation, political connections, audit market limitations and limited investor enforcement. The analysis shows that the central problem is not simply the absence of corporate governance rules, but the gap between legal design and institutional consequence. South Africa demonstrates that sophisticated governance codes can still fail where audit, board and market accountability are weak. Nigeria and Kenya show how insider lending, related-party abuse and disclosure failure can destabilise firms and financial systems. Ghana illustrates the importance of strengthening disclosure, regulator capacity and shareholder remedies as smaller capital markets deepen.
